newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Cephalon bets wrong with calls.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Cephalon bets wrong with calls.

text.p: An innovative call-buying strategy to take advantage of an expected rise in its share price turned against drug company Cephalon Inc Friday as the shares fell sharply, traders said.
Late Thursday, a Food and Drug Administration advisory panel rejected the company's Myotrophin drug for Lou Gehrig's disease, which it developed with Chiron Corp.
At around 1300 CDT/1800 GMT, Cephalon shares were down 7-1/4 at 12-3/4 on turnover of about 7.1 million shares. The stock reached a new year low at 11-1/2.
Chiron lost 1-1/8 to 18-7/8 on about 1.7 million shares.

In early April, Cephalon said it arranged to purchase call options representing the right to acquire up to 2.5 million common shares in order to benefit from any appreciation in the market value of the stock.
To pay for the issue, the company said it planned to issue up to 500,000 shares of common stock.

"It sounds like they leveraged themselves," said Michael Schwartz, managing director at Oppenheimer & Co. "If they just replaced the 500,000 shares with 5,000 options, they still would have preserved proceeds."
In the listed options market, one options contract represents 100 shares of the underlying security.
At the time Cephalon announced its arrangement to buy the calls, traders said the company probably did it because it was confident it would receive FDA approval for Myotrophin.
"They bet the farm and lost," Schwartz said.
A Cephalon spokesman said it was too early to comment on the call position.
"We did complete the transaction but it would be premature for us to comment," he said. He said the options have a strike price of 21-1/2 and a six-month term, expiring in November.
Schwartz said given the six-month time horizon, the company could cut its losses from the call position if the stock recovers.
The arrangement touched off increased interest in listed Cephalon calls and drove implied volatility sharply higher.
Cephalon options trade on the American Stock Exchange and the Chicago Board Options Exchange.

On Friday, implied volatility in Cephalon options in the May, June and August series was down from extremely high levels reached ahead of the FDA advisory panel ruling, but remained fairly steep, in many cases above 100 percent.
Historical volatility was around 77 percent.
"It's come down because it was astronomical," one floor broker in Chicago said of Cephalon implied volatility.

He said investors who were short the May out-of-the-money calls were buying them back at low prices, taking profits and exiting positions. In addition, long put holders were selling and taking profits there.
The floor broker said some institutions were buying some low-priced longer-dated calls "to take a cheap shot" on a rebound in the stock.
